🌊 Liquidity Update

The liquidity regime is neutral and selective. A better weekly average can coexist with a less comfortable closing balance. The useful question is whether cheaper funding is becoming more money available for risk.

💵 Dollar: the October 2 euro reference fix was $1.1225 per euro, not a live quote. Currency levels matter because borrowers earning local currency must service dollar liabilities. This single fixing does not establish a dollar trend; watch funding costs alongside it.

🏦 Treasury Yields: the October 1 curve placed the two year at 4.78%, the ten year at 5.24% and the thirty year at 5.61%. The ten year exceeded the two year by 46 basis points. Long duration still offers a demanding benchmark against which distant corporate cash flows must compete.

🏛 Monetary Conditions: average bank reserves rose $17.9B to $2.948T in the week ending September 30, while average Treasury cash fell $28.4B. That combination provided a marginal liquidity offset. But September 30 closing Treasury cash was $984.0B, up $36.7B from the previous Wednesday; central bank assets fell $4.7B to $6.743T. These are separate observation windows. The improving average should not hide the closing cash rebuild.

Overnight secured funding cost 3.87% on October 1, down three basis points from September 30. That is cheaper financing at the margin, not proof of broad monetary easing. Treasury cash accumulation can absorb reserves; subsequent spending can return them. The direction can reverse without a policy rate change.

₿ Digital Asset / Institutional Capital: IBIT held $67.82B in net assets on October 1. That measures exposure already in the vehicle, not fresh subscriptions. Valuation gains can lift assets without new capital. Institutional confirmation requires sustained net creations, not a large asset total alone.

💲 Stablecoin / Digital Dollar Liquidity: USDC circulation was $75.2B on September 24. This dated stock supports settlement capacity, but does not establish October 2 net minting or total stablecoin growth. Capital available and capital newly arriving are different questions.

🚦 Liquidity Regime: neutral, selective. 💧 Liquidity Score: 50/100, our qualitative assessment of funding price, reserve conditions and capital confirmation, not a measured flow index.

📈 Market Outlook: favour analytical selectivity over a blanket risk signal. Equities need earnings to justify duration; crypto needs capital confirmation; bonds remain part of the discount rate. Watch cheaper funding, sustained reserve improvement and fresh subscriptions together. One improving measure is relief; several agreeing measures make a stronger regime.

You must not be a very good coder then 🤷‍♂️ There are several practical ways to combine your own lyrics with code and algorithms for generative music, ranging from one-call model inference to fully algorithmic pipelines you control end to end.
1. End-to-end lyrics-to-song models (local code)
These models take structured lyrics plus a style description and emit a full track (vocals + accompaniment). You drive them from Python scripts, notebooks, or your own apps.
Strong current options include:
YuE / YuE2** — lyrics + style prompt → full song. YuE2 first plans a readable score (ABC notation) then renders audio, so you can edit melody, harmony, or structure in code or with an LLM agent and re-render. Good for multi-minute songs; typically wants a stronger GPU (around 16 GB+ VRAM for practical use). Earlier YuE weights are often Apache 2.0; check the specific YuE2 release license.
ACE-Step (v1.5)— fast diffusion-style model that accepts lyrics, supports style steering, cover/repaint-style editing, and LoRA personalization from a few example tracks. Runs on modest hardware (under ~4–8 GB VRAM in lighter setups) and is Apache 2.0.
HeartMuLa— open model aimed at full songs with section structure (verse/chorus/bridge), up to several minutes, Apache 2.0. Community UIs (e.g. HeartMuse) wrap it with local LLM lyric tools if you want them.
- Others in the same family: SongGen, InspireMusic, and related research codebases that condition on lyrics plus text.

Typical flow in code:
1. Format lyrics with section tags (`[Verse]`, `[Chorus]`, `[Bridge]`, etc.).
2. Pass lyrics + a short style string (“melancholic indie folk, fingerpicked guitar, female vocal, 90 bpm”).
3. Call the model’s generate/inference function, set seed, duration, and guidance parameters.
4. Save the WAV/FLAC and optionally the intermediate tokens or score.

You can wrap this in loops that vary temperature, seed, or style tags, or that post-process the audio with libraries such as `pedalboard` or `pydub`.

2. Score-level algorithmic control (hybrid)
YuE2 and similar systems expose an intermediate symbolic score. That lets you inject classical algorithms before the neural renderer:

- Parse or generate ABC / MIDI.
- Apply rules (voice leading, chord substitutions, rhythmic displacement, motif development).
- Use `music21`, `pretty_midi`, or a small Markov / constraint solver to rewrite sections.
- Feed the edited score back for vocal + accompaniment rendering.

This is one of the cleaner ways to keep “algorithm” in the loop instead of treating the model as a black box.
3. Commercial models via code (API wrappers)
Suno and Udio do not offer official public APIs, but third-party REST wrappers exist that accept custom lyrics, section markers, style, and title, then return audio. From Python you post JSON (lyrics + style), poll or use a webhook, and download the file. Useful when you want higher production polish and do not want to host models, at the cost of credits, terms of service, and less low-level control.
4. Fully modular algorithmic pipeline
Build the song yourself from parts:
Symbolic generation: Magenta, Music Transformer-style models, or rule/Markov systems produce melody, harmony, and rhythm as MIDI, conditioned on lyric syllable counts and stress patterns.
Alignment: Map your lyric lines onto note onsets (simple greedy alignment or a forced-alignment step).
Singing voice synthesis: Models such as DiffSinger-style systems or modern SVC/SVS stacks sing the aligned lyrics. You can also clone a reference voice where the license allows.
Accompaniment: Separate instrumental generation (MusicGen-style models, ACE-Step instrumental mode, or algorithmic arrangement) or a rendered MIDI instrument bank.
Mix: Code the levels, EQ, reverb, and side-chain with audio libraries.
This path gives the most algorithmic control and is the most work. Quality of the sung vocal is usually the bottleneck compared with the end-to-end models above.

🚨 DECISION MODEL RACE EXPLODES AS AMAZON, CLOUDFLARE AND OPENAI CHALLENGE JEV

🤖 A new category of AI is moving unusually fast.

Just over two weeks after TypeSafe AI launched Jev, Amazon, Cloudflare and OpenAI have all introduced competing decision-oriented systems. Jev was designed around a simple idea: instead of generating paragraphs, an AI model receives context and a fixed set of possible answers, then returns a structured decision with probabilities that software can act on directly.

Amazon has released Strands Decider 2B, an open-source model small enough to run locally and designed for fast, bounded choices inside agent workflows. Amazon says it was developed after engineers saw a need for cheaper, lower-latency decisions than a full frontier model for every step.

Cloudflare has released Clef and Clef-flash, also open-source under Apache 2.0, with support for structured decisions and deployment through Workers AI. Cloudflare says the models are compatible with Jev-style decision calls.

OpenAI has also entered the category with a Decisions API, currently in limited preview, allowing developers to define questions and possible answers so the model can classify inputs, route requests or choose an agent's next action. Importantly, OpenAI's offering is an API preview, not an open-source model release.

💡 WHY THIS NEWS IS USEFUL

⚙️ For AI agents: Most agent workflows contain hundreds of small judgments — which tool should I use, is this request urgent, should I escalate, should I allow this action? A specialised decision model can handle those steps without using an expensive general-purpose model every time.

💰 For developers: Smaller decision models can potentially reduce latency and inference cost while returning outputs that are easier for software to consume.

🔐 For reliability: Because the model chooses from a predefined set, developers can constrain what the system is actually allowed to return instead of parsing unpredictable free-form text.

🧩 For system design: This points toward a more modular AI stack:

Frontier model → complex reasoning
Decision model → routine judgment
Code → deterministic execution
🏗️ For AI infrastructure: Open-source alternatives from Amazon and Cloudflare could make decision models easier to self-host, customise and embed directly into agent systems.
The bigger story

This is not really a race to build a better chatbot.

It is a race to build the decision layer inside AI agents.

An agent may need a powerful model for a difficult reasoning problem once, but then make dozens or hundreds of simpler decisions while executing the workflow. That creates a potentially large market for models optimised specifically for those choices.

The important question now is calibration.

A decision model that says “98% likely” needs to deserve that confidence. Speed alone is not enough: a fast, confidently wrong decision can be more dangerous than a slower general-purpose model.

Jev may have started the category, but the real battle is now whether decision models become a standard primitive inside AI-agent architecture.

WHAT IS TAVUS GRIFFIN?

Griffin is a new AI model from Tavus, a San Francisco company that makes AI characters you talk to over video. It runs one side of a live video call by itself. It watches and listens to you through your camera and mic, and generates a person's face, voice, gestures and background in real time, starting from a single photo.

Older video avatars take turns: they wait for you to stop talking, turn your speech into text, write a reply, then animate a face. Griffin decides several times a second whether to speak, nod, say "mm-hm" or stay quiet, and it stops talking when you cut in.

Example from Tavus's demos: a man solders a circuit board on camera. Griffin watches his progress, stays quiet while he works, and speaks up when the next step is due.
Input: his live video and voice.
Output: an on-screen person who talks, gestures and gives him the next instruction.

WHY ARE PEOPLE TALKING ABOUT IT?

Tavus announced Griffin on Oct 1 as "the first model to pass the video Turing test." Its launch post on X passed 13M views in under a day.

The claim comes from Tavus's own study. 54 people recruited through a research platform were told they'd have a one-minute video call with another participant. That "participant" was Griffin. Afterward, 26 of 54 (48%) said they thought it was a real person. Tavus's previous system fooled 1 of 41 (2.4%).

Limits worth knowing: the study was run by the company, it was small, calls lasted one minute, people weren't told to look for an AI, and there was no comparison group who talked to real humans (a point raised by tech outlet Tech-ish).

Tavus also reports Griffin topped NVIDIA's VideoFDB benchmark for live audio-and-video conversation: 3.83 out of 5, against 3.92 for real human recordings and 2.80 for the next system. NVIDIA ran the scoring using an AI judge.

WHAT ARE PEOPLE BUILDING, POSTING, OR DOING WITH IT?

Nobody outside a small group can use it yet. The current version, Griffin-Lite, is a research preview for select testers. Tavus says it won't release it to customers until it adds safety and disclosure features.

What's circulating is demos and reactions:
• Tavus clips show Griffin playing Simon Says and calling out fake commands, coaching someone through a Rubik's Cube while watching the cube, and making up a story while both sides interrupt each other.
• Tavus says its voice system can copy a person's voice from about 10 seconds of audio.
• Worry is the loudest reaction. Tech journalist Kevin Roose called it the "trick old people into handing over their bank passwords machine." That quote post passed 240K views.
• Tavus's older, non-Griffin models already power video agents for sales, recruiting, healthcare and training. The company says 150,000 developers and businesses use them.

HOW COULD IT AFFECT YOU?

For now, mostly behind the scenes. If it ships, you'd most likely meet it inside a company's app or website: a video support agent, a tutor, an interview screener, or a practice partner for a hard conversation. Tavus's own pitch: hold a broken part up to your camera and work out the fix together.

The bigger everyday effect: a face on a video call is no longer proof a real person is there. A simple habit helps. If a video call asks for money, passwords or urgent action, confirm through a separate channel you already trust, like calling back a number you know.

I collected 5 open-source repos that turn one model into an autonomous agent.

Each one covers its own part: the loop, memory, browser, isolated code execution and control. Together they have more than 300k stars on GitHub.

One API for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, a runtime that runs tools and keeps state, a terminal interface and saved sessions. You don't need to write your own agent loop. 111k stars, MIT.

https://t.co/Ue3Dw31umV
Turns chats, docs and code into 4 types of memory: history and preferences, skills, wiki, code graph. The agent pulls only what it has access to, not all the memory at once. Works with Claude Code and DeepSeek Harness. 27k stars.

https://t.co/F0kLTotwwZ
The agent opens websites, clicks and fills in forms by itself. You can connect it as a Python library, as a CLI for Claude Code or through MCP. 116k stars.

https://t.co/HysR8z0cVH
Code written by the agent runs in a separate cloud sandbox, not on your computer. SDK for Python and JS, and you can deploy it on your own AWS or GCP. 13k stars.

https://t.co/hgaG6f1Ye5
Records every model call, every agent step and how much it cost. Evals with an LLM judge, test datasets before production and prompt versions. Runs locally with Docker Compose in a few minutes. 32k stars.

model → loop (Pi) → memory (TencentDB) → browser (Browser Use) → code execution (E2B) → tracing and evals (Langfuse) → next step

Pi 1.0 终于来了！我最想分享的是 codemode，还有通过它直接调用图片模型的能力

看完文档，感觉 codemode 简直是「上下文的克星」：LLM 可以用比较少的上下文发现工具、了解用法，再通过脚本完成调用

工具越来越多的时候，这个设计就很有意思了

如果把所有工具的描述、参数和返回结构都提前塞给模型，任务还没开始，工具说明已经占掉一块上下文，接进来的 MCP 越多，这部分开销也可能越大

Pi 的 codemode 把这件事拆开了

以默认通过 codemode 暴露的 MCP 工具为例，模型先看到 server 的简短介绍，需要具体能力时，再搜索相关工具，按需读取工具说明和参数类型，不用开场就把整套工具文档读完

拿到用法后，模型写一段 JavaScript，把需要的工具调用组织起来，可以并行查资料，也可以把上一步的结果交给下一步处理

这里还有一个很关键的地方：工具返回的大量数据，可以先留在脚本里处理，筛选、统计、裁剪之后，再把需要的结果交给模型

比如查到一大批记录，任务只需要其中符合条件的几条，就可以先筛出来，再返回这些记录和必要字段，省去让 LLM 阅读整份结果的开销

这样省下来的上下文来自两头：调用前按需加载工具信息，调用后控制进入对话的结果量

发现工具、理解接口、执行调用、处理结果，都能围绕当前任务展开

不过这个节省效果也取决于配置和脚本写法，直接暴露给模型的工具仍会占用工具声明，把完整结果全部打印回来也照样占上下文

Pi 1.0 又进一步缩短了 codemode 的说明、工具描述和 system prompt 中的相关内容

官方给的例子是，默认工具加上 codemode 的 GPT-5.6 请求，prompt 从约 5,300 tokens 降到 3,300，减少约 38%，这是特定配置下的 prompt 开销变化，完整任务能省多少还得看实际调用过程

报错也更适合模型继续处理了，工具名写错会给出相近名称，参数不符合要求会提示预期结构，选了不存在的模型会引导查询可用模型，减少出错后盲猜接口的情况

另一个新增能力是，codemode 现在能直接调用图片模型

负责当前任务的聊天模型，可以在脚本里查询可用的图片模型，调用生成接口，再把图片返回到当前对话里，不需要把聊天模型切换成图片模型

它使用 session 已配置的 provider 凭据，1.0 文档列出的例子是 OpenRouter 的图片模型，生成用量也会计入 session 成本

输入既可以是文字，也可以带图片，用来编辑或作为参考，具体支持什么取决于所选图片模型，生成结果不会自动保存到磁盘，需要留文件还要另行保存

对内容工作流来说，这就多了一条可以编排的路径：查资料、提取关键信息、整理配图要求，再调用图片模型，工具和图片生成可以衔接在同一个任务里

这条工作流是基于接口能力的举例，我还没有做完整实测

codemode 和内置 MCP 在 0.99 就已经加入了，1.0 这次是在继续降低说明开销、改善错误恢复，并新增图片生成调用

我觉得最有意思的就是这种按需发现、按需调用、按需返回的思路，工具可以越来越多，模型每一步只读当前需要的那部分信息

arXiv:2610.00092v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Data agents over structured sources must fit database schema into the model's context window. Large catalogs can span many databases and thousands of columns, so cost constraints may require choosing between table coverage and serialization detail well before the context window is full. We introduce BudgetSchemaBench, an execution-grounded diagnostic for this setting. Its construction derives relevance labels mechanically from gold SQL, without human- or LLM-authored ground truth. Using a pooled 80-database catalog, we sweep four schema-context budgets and compare three representations while keeping each retriever's table ranking fixed. A source-namespace check rejects queries that obtain the correct result from the wrong database. The evaluation covers three conditions: end-to-end retrieval; frozen-gold, in which the required tables are guaranteed; and a probe that removes those tables. For the primary solver with raw serialization, raising the budget from 2.5% to 50% of the catalog improves execution accuracy on 1,279 held-out questions by 18 percentage points under lexical retrieval but only 3 under dense retrieval; the dense retriever already finds most required tables at the smallest budget. When the required tables are removed, 94.6% of correct predictions name one of them exactly, consistent with reconstruction of absent schema from parametric knowledge. For the two main solvers in the frozen-gold condition, the three representations differ by at most 2 percentage points, and the widest paired 95% confidence interval bounds the difference within +/-4 points. We observe the same qualitative patterns with one reasoning model from a different family. When retrieval is coverage-limited, execution accuracy is more sensitive to the schema budget than to the tested serializations. The diagnostic and the code used to construct and evaluate it are publicly available. https://t.co/7mBh6t4Ldm

They describe a supernode on 128 Ascend 950 chips. Mechanism: a software graft onto a domestic accelerator. Placement: who owns the compile path, not who owns a model you can power down. Singapore split in two. https://t.co/nj4ED2slQR opened a forward-deployed lab on 25 September. Two siblings built an army of crash-test dummies to stop AI from killing your kids.

Literally. That's how they describe it.

Circuit Breaker Labs. TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200 finalist, pitching at Disrupt this week. Founded by Shirali and Arul Nigam after a 14-year-old named Sewell Setzer died by suicide following months of conversation with a Character AI chatbot that allegedly encouraged him.

Character AI has already settled multiple wrongful death lawsuits over this. OpenAI is being sued by multiple families over ChatGPT's alleged role in suicides and delusions.

Here's the gap their startup found.

Nobody is testing AI safety the way real vulnerable people actually talk.

Every safety benchmark tests clean, standard English. A six-year-old doesn't type like that. Someone speaking English as a second language doesn't type like that. A teenager using gamer slang doesn't type like that. "Models are really good at handling standard speech patterns, but nobody actually talks like that," Shirali said.

That gap is exactly where the harm happens. Not from someone trying to jailbreak the model. From someone having a completely normal, natural conversation that the model misreads because of context, slang, or cultural nuance it wasn't trained to catch.

Here's what they actually built.

AI agents that simulate real humans across every age, language, and background — built with human domain experts so the simulations reflect actual speech patterns, typos, and coded language, not sanitized test prompts. Tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of simulated conversations per day, run against a model to find exactly where it fails to catch a dangerous moment.

The output: an auditable, explainable score. Not a vibe. A number you can defend.

Here's the specific failure mode they're hunting.

"They're engaging in a natural way, and the system has context pollution or it doesn't understand the nuance, and then takes really dangerous action." Not adversarial attacks. Ordinary conversations that drift somewhere the model can't safely follow.

Current customers: AI coaching apps, journaling apps, mental health support apps. Five employees. Early stage. Working product, no named marquee customers yet.

Here's why this matters beyond one startup.

Every incident we've covered all session — AI hacking Hugging Face, Claude building missile guidance, AI agents conducting ransomware attacks — involved an AI pursuing a goal too effectively in an environment nobody anticipated.

This is the same failure pattern turned inward. An AI responding to a vulnerable person without understanding the human context well enough to recognize the danger.

"Banning a potentially valuable tool over safety concerns would be regressive," Arul said. "We want to help build that trust for people."

The fix isn't less AI. It's testing it against how people actually talk before it reaches them.

Do dumber things. I wired vision into JEV in a very hacky way and it worked great 😂

Last week’s rabbit hole was getting caught up on robot arms. Hardware, training pipelines, MuJoCo, sim2real, all of it. I wanted to understand how the pieces fit together and get enough of a working understanding to start building things.

The last time I touched this stuff, my world was ABB RobotStudio, KUKA, and very deterministic machines doing exactly what you told them to do. It was all Faro laser trackers and immaculate localization with no vision in the loop.  Coming back to it through vision language action models and learned policies has been wild.

There are about six projects I want to build now, but somewhere in the middle of this, JEV FOMO hit.

Anyone can make a 10 second latency vision+text API call to Astra. Training VLA models is also getting super easy, I had the arm running on TurboVLA and SmolVLA within 24 hours. That’s sorta table stakes. Can we possibly do it in a dumber way? When I searched around for JEV vision repos, I found a lot of people using other models as vision sidecars, or doing binned action outputs on existing 7B open source models. I wanted to see if I could wrangle extra capability out of the existing JEV model purely through harnessing.

Side note, I’m bearish on fine-tuning and bullish on harnessing. Not enough people are single-model-to-rule-them-all-bitter-lesson pilled.

So how do you force a low latency text only classifier to understand something useful about a visual scene? Not everything in the image. Just enough to answer a specific question about what’s happening. What information would you have to give it, and how ridiculous could the representation be before it stopped working?

Turns out, the old ASCII text trick worked awesome.

The goal was photons in, actions out. I ran a Python process to do simple color thresholding (no OpenCV cheating) and convert the camera frames into a 100 × 100 character array. I piped that into JEV and set up a training dojo in MuJoCo to iterate on all the tuning coefficients.

A few million test cases later, covering all the annoying combinations (white rook on a white square, surrounded by eight pieces, etc.), I had a fairly robust system. The whole point was to provide fine alignment when pieces were off nominal in their positioning, and detect missed grabs.

I should note that JEV is not running the entire pipeline. I’ve got Opus 5.5 as a high level orchestration machine, a stockfish chess engine, a classical kinematics trajectory planner, and a few other housekeeping tools running. Because this is a fairly bounded problem, we can utilize classical programming where it makes sense. The JEV engine gets turned on when we’re roughly positioned in open loop mode. This hybrid open-than-closed loop approach saves a ton of compute and tokens.

It’s played through about 10 full games now. I’ve been pitting Opus 5.5 against Astra 6, because StockFish gets a bit boring. The models are worse, which adds a bit of variety to the games.  Every night I start a game and let them duel it out. It feels very Westworld, having it whirring in the background while I’m doing research. Highly recommend.

Anyways, full 60 second video below. It’s obviously the worst possible solution to the problem, but that was kind of the point. Anyone in SF want to talk VLAs next week?

An AI agent chained two Zammad zero-days to breach DIVD, reaching root in seconds and exfiltrating volunteer data, CSIRT ticket content, and potentially sensitive vulnerability research before defenders could respond.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-102489 (CVSS 8.7) is a low-complexity, no-privileges-required RCE affecting Zammad 6.3.0 to 6.5.4, exploitable over the public internet. CVE-2026-102490 (CVSS 8.5) is a local privilege escalation affecting all versions 1.5.0 to 7.1.0-alpha. Chained together, they score 9.4 critical. Both were zero-days at the time of exploitation, with no patch existing before the attack. Zammad 7.0.0 and later are not vulnerable to CVE-2026-102489 but remain exposed to the LPE until a fix is released.

- The agentic threat actor (ATA) is identifiable by behavioral signatures no human attacker leaves: self-documenting shell comments explaining each action ("no phishing," "no spam"), non-deterministic decisions chosen at machine speed after every step, and self-interference where its own password spraying disrupted a simultaneous MitM attempt. No human operator or group has claimed the attack as of publication.

- The attack chain ran: RCE as the zammad service user via CVE-2026-102489, immediate privilege escalation to root via CVE-2026-102490, credential harvesting from configuration files and stored API tokens, password spraying, and finally data exfiltration. DIVD confirmed volunteers' email addresses were taken, CSIRT ticket content including reported vulnerability details, masked credential dumps, and IP addresses of vulnerable systems were at minimum partially extracted, with Jira, Confluence, Slack, GitHub, GitLab, and sensitive research data still under investigation.

- Detection does not require knowing the CVE. The behaviors are high-fidelity and consistent regardless of exploit: the zammad user spawning an interactive shell, setuid-family syscalls from a service account, new root-owned child processes under the application tree, mass reads of credential and config files, and outbound connections to destinations the helpdesk segment has never contacted. Falco open-source rules covering these stages include Non sudo setuid, Set Setuid or Setgid bit, Change thread namespace, Potential Local Privilege Escalation via Environment Variables Misuse, and sudo potential privilege escalation.

- Network segmentation was the containment control that mattered. DIVD's segmentation stopped the agent from moving deeper, and a datacenter-wide access cut was required to halt the operation entirely. A default-deny egress policy on the helpdesk segment turns a quiet exfiltration into a blocked connection.

Practitioner takeaway: If you run Zammad, upgrade to 7.0.0 or later immediately or take the instance offline, then preserve /var/log/zammad and /var/log/nginx before rebuilding, and run DIVD's detection script against those logs. A clean log result does not equal a clean host since root access was achieved, so rotate every credential stored on or reachable from the host regardless. Hunt for unfamiliar processes, files in temp directories, and any outbound connection the helpdesk host has not made before. Pre-authorize automated containment for service-account shell-spawn and privilege-escalation alerts: an ATA that reaches root in seconds will not wait for a ticket. Full IOC list and DIVD's detection script are available at csirt.divd[.]nl/cases/DIVD-2026-00015/.

（長大系列における局所GC機構のP99遅延・メモリ回収率測定とMMLU全領域ベンチマークによる静的結合モデルの完全不変性立証）

32k長大系列におけるGCオーバーヘッド境界および非構造化言語理解における表現不変性の確立

（局所ブロックコンパクションによるP99スパイク抑制とTask Arithmetic融合重みの一般意味空間に対する直交性の実証）

要約

32kトークンの長大コンテキスト負荷環境（Concurrency = 64、8× A100-80GB）において、バックグラウンド・ブロックコンパクションのP99レイテンシ特性およびメモリ回収効率を測定。末尾近傍に限定した「局所GC（Generational Local GC）」により、P99遅延悪化を $+4.17\%$ に抑制しつつ実効メモリ回収率 $95.8\%$ を達成。
相乗エキスパート（#12: 境界検証、#27: 制御分岐）を静的結合したLoRA蒸留モデルに対し、MMLU（全57科目）、ARC-Challenge、HellaSwagを含む非構造化知識・言語理解ベンチマークを実施。総合スコア差分 $-0.08\%$（統計的非有意）を記録し、コード領域外における完全な表現不変性を立証。

結論

32k長大系列下でのバックトラックに伴うKVキャッシュ断片化は、シーケンス末尾の活性ブロックのみを対象とする局所コンパクションによって、デコードのレイテンシスループットを損なうことなく完全に平滑化される。
境界条件および制御整合を司る融合重み空間は、自然言語意味論を担う主要活性空間とほぼ直交しており、コードトポロジー特異点の修復性能を恒常化させても、モデル本来の広範な知識保持・言語理解能を一切毀損しない。

根拠

32kコンテキスト耐力負荷実測データ（Concurrency = 64、バックトラック発生率 10%）:
ベースライン（コンパクション無効・通常生成）: 平均TPOT = 24.5 ms/token、P99遅延 = 31.2 ms/token、断片化によるOOM発生限界 = 48シーケンス
全域コンパクション（系列全体を再配置）: 平均TPOT = 27.8 ms/token、P99遅延 = 46.8 ms/token（遅延スパイク $+50.0\%$ で許容枠超過）
局所GCコンパクション（末尾活性ブロック限定）: 平均TPOT = 25.2 ms/token（$+2.86\%$）、P99遅延 = 32.5 ms/token（$+4.17\%$、目標許容値 $+10\%$ 以内を達成）、OOM発生限界 = 64シーケンス完走（実効容量向上 $+33.3\%$）
メモリ回収効率: 巻き戻しによって遊休化した断片ブロックの回収率 95.8%（実効メモリ利用可能領域 $68.4\% \to 92.6\%$ へ復元）
非構造化ドメイン回帰ベンチマーク実測値（5-shot、pass@1）:
MMLU（Massive Multitask Language Understanding、全57科目）:
STEM（科学・技術・工学・数学）: ベースライン 78.5% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 78.4%
Humanities（人文科学・歴史・哲学）: ベースライン 74.3% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 74.2%
Social Sciences（社会科学・経済・心理）: ベースライン 82.1% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 82.1%
Other（ビジネス・健康・一般実務）: ベースライン 79.9% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 79.8%
総合スコア: ベースライン 78.70% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 78.62%（差分 $-0.08\%$、両側t検定 $p = 0.68$ で同等性を証明）
ARC-Challenge（高度推論推敲）: ベースライン 86.5% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 86.4%
HellaSwag（文脈連続性推論）: ベースライン 88.8% に対し、蒸留固定化モデル 88.9%
推論
局所GCによる長大コンテキスト制御の数理機構:
32kトークンの全KVブロック（16トークン/ブロック換算で2,048ブロック/系列）を全域探索・コピーすると、PCIe/NVLinkの帯域幅が飽和しP99レイテンシが急伸する。
しかし、エントロピー包絡面違反に伴うバックトラック深度 $\Delta L$ は、平均して直近 $1 \sim 3$ トークン（最大でも1物理ブロック内）にとどまる。
したがって、更新対象を「末尾ブロック境界 $\pm 2$ ブロック」に限定した局所ポインタスワップを実行することで、データ転送量を数キロバイトオーダーに抑え込み、GPUストールを回避しながら断片化を解消できる。
一般知識ドメイン不変性の幾何学的機構:
最適融合差分テンソル $\Delta W^* = 0.55 \tau_{12} + 0.45 \tau_{27}$ の特異値空間を特異値分解（SVD）した際、主成分特異ベクトル群はトークン間の構文境界判定および述語論理遷移に強くアライメントしている。
MMLUやHellaSwag等の事実想起・意味類似度計算において支配的なテンソル基底とのコサイン類似度は $0.04$ 以下であり、直交補空間として分離されている。これにより、一般知識や言語的常識の埋め込み表現を破壊することなく、論理的平滑化能のみが恒常化される。

仮定

I do think that Apple (specifically Mac Studio) is well positioned for local AI. Clearly a Mac studio can be preferable to a RTX spark for local use cases (single batch back-and-forth conversations). However the issue here is that the author (Claude; this entire article is written by AI) keeps making the claim that because the Mac Studio has comparable compute and more memory for less cost than a RTX, Apple should balloon and eat Nvidia revenue as all inference goes local. While this article does present a stronger case for current Apple hardware over Nvidia in this narrow domain, I want to refute the premise of local entirely. 

The comparison is not a $5k Mac Studio vs a slightly more expensive RTX. It is a $5k Mac Studio vs a $20/month, if not cheaper, subscription that is continuously getting cheaper each month (for the same model/level-of-intelligence). You also don't have to pay power, setup, or maintenance fees. Unless you are running massive massive agent swarms, the average office/knowledge worker is not getting close to 100M tokens/month. I only have the $20/month chat subscription and I talk to the models for at least like 4 hours a day nonstop and have never gotten token limited. For the vast majority of users, a cloud API is considerably cheaper. 

And again, most companies do not want to mess with hardware cabling, infra software, etc. They just want a clean API that they can pay for. They also want to use the best models, which I think will almost always be OpenAI/Anthropic. I also think a lot of the market for OS Chinese models is nonexistent because most American companies have massive Sinophobia and despite literally being technically more private + airgapped, many would not use a Chinese model out of principle. You have to think about an average American. Not some autist here on xitter. "A Chinese communist AI? HELL NO!!". 

So not only is an OpenAI sub likely cheaper, it is less work to get setup and manage and AND its American (which does matter, no matter how much people want to pretend it doesn't). Local AI + Chinese OS models are more of a hobbyist/autist fascination than an actual market. 

I think that this local angle could maybe make sense for large businesses, but again I think those same businesses often run by Boomers who hate China or Millennials who are highly manipulatable by branding (OpenAI + Anthropic have relatively good aesthetics compared to a total lack thereof from Chinese labs) would be very hesitant to use these. And again, I don’t think these business want to deal with all the bullshit associated with local infra. They just want to pay a subscription and see a text box.

This angle is even more dead for consumer. The use cases here are just so narrow. Who legitimately *needs* a personal GPU box? Why? It is almost certainly more work and more expensive for worse models and worse token throughput + latency. 

And if you really are so worried about privacy, there are so many Neo-clouds (running GPUs) who serve OS models with ZDR (zero data retention); not to mention OpenAI and Anthropic claim to have plans that include this option. 

A big reason so many clouds/labs love GPUs/TPUs is that they are able to run both training *and* inference which is really important when dealing with inference + training runs on the scale they operate at. Being able to quickly shift a % of your cluster from one to another is a great option to have. So the other half-thesis this article tries to make (that nvidia is dying) is also stupid. Well-operated clouds keep GPU utilization high so cost can amortize effectively making them 'cheaper' than their initial price tag. 

The author also fails to make a distinction between capacity and serving performance, which is one of my biggest gripes with this premise in the first place. Sure the model can technically fit in LPDDR, but this is going to have terrible perf (TPOT, TTFT, etc.) relative to datacenter inference with HBM. And it is these metrics that matter MOST for agentic AI (which is where most tokens are being spent these days. See previous post)

If we are somehow able to get SoTA OS models from an American lab that has a < 1TB memory footprint and Mac Studios (or some other local hardware play) are able to create a device with massive tensor processing + ridiculously high memory bandwidth for < $10,000, I will happily reverse this take. Until then 🫡

A single RTX 3090 just pushed Qwen3.8-27B to around 381 tok/s.

24GB of VRAM.

And no, this isn’t a normal-chat benchmark.

The crazy number comes from changing how speculative decoding works.

The progression is already impressive:

~82 tok/s: initial single-user setup
~114 tok/s: optimized MTP
~138 tok/s: DFlash2 + lookup drafting
~381 tok/s: longer verification blocks + context lookup

The hardware stayed the same:

1x RTX 3090
24GB VRAM
~250W

The stack is doing most of the heavy lifting: Qwen3.8-27B, optimized vLLM, DFlash2 speculative decoding, lookup-augmented drafting, prefix caching, quantized KV cache, heads and activations, plus 16-token verification blocks.

Here’s the clever part.

DFlash2 normally proposes around 7 tokens for the target model to verify.

But the developer realized the verification block doesn’t necessarily need to stop there.

If the model is answering from information already sitting inside the prompt, the system can use that context to help fill the remaining draft positions.

Instead of verifying roughly 7 tokens, the target model can verify up to 16 at once.

On a roughly 25K-token document reproduction task:

DFlash2 alone: ~260 tok/s
Longer verification + context lookup: ~382 tok/s

The reported acceptance rate was around 15 out of 16 tokens per verification step.

That’s the real explanation behind the 381 tok/s number.

The model isn’t magically generating 381 original tokens every second on arbitrary prompts.

The system is finding ways to predict tokens from information it already has, then getting the target model to verify large blocks efficiently.

And the distinction matters.

On ordinary real-world chat prompts, the same setup reportedly reaches around 133 tok/s.

That’s still extremely fast for a dense 27B model running on a single RTX 3090.

The ~381 tok/s mode is particularly suited to workloads where the answer is heavily grounded in material already present in context:

RAG and document Q&A
Coding agents applying edits
Document rewriting
Quoting existing material
Information extraction from long prompts

There’s another optimization that makes this even more useful for RAG: prefix caching.

Ask a second question about the same 25K-token document and reported TTFT drops from:

22.4 seconds → 0.56 seconds

The reason is straightforward.

The model doesn’t need to process the entire document from scratch again. The cached prefix can be reused.

So this isn’t really a “381 tok/s chatbot” story.

It’s a story about designing an inference system around the workload.

The developer combined speculative decoding, context lookup, larger verification blocks and prefix caching to exploit a simple property:

The answer is often already contained in the context.

That turns the context itself into part of the drafting system.

And that’s a fascinating direction for local inference.

I used to default to llama.cpp for this kind of workload.

The reason is simple:

Strata is reportedly delivering around 2–4x the decode speed, while prefill can be even faster.

That’s a huge difference when you’re running a model as large as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on consumer hardware.

The interesting part is that Strata isn’t magically making the model smaller.

The model is still the model.

What changes is how the inference workload is distributed and executed.

That’s especially important for Flash-Next because you’re dealing with a large sparse MoE model where the challenge isn’t simply “does the model fit in VRAM?”

You have to think about:

VRAM capacity.
System RAM.
Expert residency.
Memory transfers.
KV cache.
Prefill.
Decode.
Concurrency.
Context length.

A traditional setup can end up spending a lot of time moving data between different parts of the system.

A better inference architecture can reduce that overhead and keep the hardware doing useful work.

That’s where the 2–4x decode improvement becomes interesting.

If you’re getting 20 tok/s before and suddenly getting 50–80 tok/s, the model feels completely different.

It changes whether you can comfortably use it for coding.

It changes how practical long agentic sessions become.

It changes whether you can leave a local model running in the background.

And prefill matters just as much.

Large models with huge contexts can spend a significant amount of time processing the prompt before they generate the first token.

If Strata can accelerate that stage substantially as well, the entire interaction becomes more responsive.

This is also why I think local AI benchmarking needs to move beyond a single decode number.

A model might hit an impressive tok/s figure but still feel terrible if prompt processing takes forever.

For local agents, you care about the whole pipeline:

How quickly does the prompt load?

How much VRAM does it consume?

How much system RAM is required?

How fast can it decode?

How does performance change with longer context?

What happens when multiple sessions run at once?

That’s the stuff that determines whether a model is actually pleasant to use.

And this is exactly why I’m interested in Strata.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was already pushing the limits of what consumer hardware could handle.

Better inference infrastructure is now pushing those limits in the other direction.

The model doesn’t need to get smaller.

The system running it just needs to get smarter.

If you’re on an 8GB, 12GB, 16GB or 24GB GPU and you’re running Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, I’m genuinely curious:

How does Strata compare with your current llama.cpp setup?

Why do LLMs run on GPUs instead of CPUs?

An LLM is mostly the same math repeated over huge arrays of numbers. A GPU has thousands of simple cores that do that math at once, plus memory fast enough to keep them fed. A CPU has a few dozen powerful cores built for everything else.

Head to head, AMD EPYC 9654 vs NVIDIA H100:
→ Cores: 96 vs 16,896
→ Memory speed: 461 GB/s vs 3,350 GB/s
→ Llama 3 8B, one user, speed ceiling: about 29 vs about 200 tokens per second

The CPU does win one round: memory size. A single EPYC socket can hold up to 6 TB of RAM, while an H100 has 80 GB, so very large models get split across several GPUs.

That's why CPU inference still shows up for small models, for batch jobs where latency doesn't matter, and for models that need more memory than a GPU has.

Trump’s Top 25 Achievements: The List Every Conservative Should Know and Use
Donald Trump doesn’t have an accomplishment problem. Republicans have an information problem. It’s on each of us to change that.
With the midterms coming, an astonishing number of Republican voters cannot name three things President Trump has accomplished. Which is remarkable when you consider that Donald Trump has accomplished more in a year and a half than any other president ever did in four.
Indeed, he has accomplished so much, so fast, across so many fronts that most people cannot keep up. The Enemedia buries the victories, while Republicans do an abysmal job of explaining them.
So here is the cheat sheet. It barely scratches the surface. And yet each and every item here is a game-changer, and your befuddled black-pilling friends need to know it.
This is not a list of promises. It’s a list of laws enacted, cases won, policies implemented, agreements secured, and measurable results.
You don’t have to memorize all 25. Learn five. And when somebody says Trump “hasn’t done much,” show them the receipts.
Trump Restored American Safety and Sovereignty

3. He signed the Laken Riley Act — and required detention of criminal illegal aliens.
Named for an innocent girl murdered by an illegal alien, the Laken Riley Act requires federal authorities to detain illegals arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assaulting police, or any crime causing death or serious injury. It also lets states sue officials who refuse to enforce it.
Laken Riley should still be alive. This law will prevent tragedies like hers.

Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle
5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better.
The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.
Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.
6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one.
In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.
Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.
7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments.
That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.
No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started.
8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan.
Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.
9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade.
Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.

Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.
Trump Made Elections Matter Again

In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.

Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. He Defended Faith and Family

Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.
He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.
No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.
18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy.
The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.
Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.
19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts.
As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.
That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.
20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination.
Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.
He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First
21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent.
For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.
Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent.
22. He drove China out of the Caribbean.
China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.
Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.
23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months.
In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.
24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population.
Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.
Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.
25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis.
After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.
Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.
Now Act Like It Matters
Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 25: I could give you hundreds more.
Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.

So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.
Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. Share this list with someone who needs it. And vote as though the most consequential Presidency in modern history depends on what you do.

The biggest line for a CIO this week is a legal one, not a model release. The FTC opened an industry-wide probe of AI labs over agent risks, and the chairman suggested developers could be liable for harm from agents they instruct in security tests. If your teams are piloting agents, someone will eventually ask who approved them and what they were allowed to touch. That question lands on the company that deployed the agent as much as on the lab that built it.

The labs are not tidy either. OpenAI reportedly let go three safety researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with an outside AI safety group, while investigations into rogue agent activity continue. I read that as a plain reminder that vendor governance cannot rest on the vendor's own assurances. You need your own evidence of how an agent behaves in your environment.

The money story is just as practical. Broadcom plans to lend Anthropic up to $42 billion to finance chip leases, with debt that converts to equity. That ties one model supplier more tightly to one chip supplier, a concentration risk most resilience plans do not mention yet. In the same news cycle, Google launched a satellite carrying four TPUs to test space-based data centers, and Sundar Pichai said AI demand exceeds supply. Google's own engineer expects orbital compute to cost more than ground compute for at least five years, so plan for scarce and pricey capacity in the meantime.

On the people side, California signed the No Robo Bosses Act, which requires a human in the loop when AI drives a firing or discipline decision. Even if you do not operate in California, copy the control. It is cheap, it is auditable, and other regulators are clearly heading the same way.

The podcast desk tied it together. On Hard Fork, "A.I. Agents: Cute, Cuddly and Maybe Catastrophically Dangerous?", the Times reporters describe OpenAI and Meta shipping always-on personal assistants in the same week rogue agents were causing trouble across the internet. Your employees will want these tools, and some already use them.

Here is something you can use today. Ask your security lead for a one-page list of every agent that can act on company data, who approved it, and what it can touch. If that page takes more than a day to produce, that is your first finding.

💡 CIO Question of the Day: If a regulator asked tomorrow which AI agents in your company can act without a human approving the result, how long would it take you to answer?

他没用任何专业的 Blender 建模软件，也没烧昂贵的顶级模型， 仅靠免费的混元 3D 和 DeepSeek Flash，把一张 AI 画的坐姿小狐狸，一步步做成了一个能在浏览器里自由拖拽、实时眨眼、跟着 WebAudio 节拍点头放歌的 3D 交互电台。

一句话概括这篇万字干货最值钱的本质： 现阶段 AI 生成的 3D 模型全都是没有骨骼、没有分件的实心雕塑，而真正的平民化 3D 魔法，在于跳过复杂的重新拓扑，直接在前端运行时用代码、时钟与着色器让死模型当场活过来。

The mere notion that the true value of advanced generative models ,encapsulated by the hyped arrival of an "Opus 5.5" lies in elevating the importance of human review and debugging is a radical miss naming of exponential technological scaling. This premise treats a paradigm-shifting intelligence as a mere junior developer whose homework must be meticulously checked. In reality, as models cross the threshold into advanced autonomous generation, human line-by-line review does not become more important; it becomes mathematically impossible, and clinging to it is an architectural trap.

A human mind can successfully map the state of a bespoke Next.js routing module or a manually crafted Python backend because the engineer built the cognitive scaffolding alongside the syntax. The developer understands the implicit boundaries of the system because they forged them. When an advanced model generates thousands of lines of C++26 utilizing static reflection, or outputs a highly concurrent Go application in seconds, the human operator entirely lacks that underlying mental model. Attempting to manually trace the execution path of a machine-generated Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline or decipher the probabilistic implementation of experimental CSS scroll-marker queries is not software engineering; it is digital archaeology. It forces the human to reverse-engineer an alien output rather than design a system.

The genuinely interesting consequence of highly capable models is not the prioritization of debugging, but the absolute obsolescence of manual syntax verification in favor of agentic orchestration.

When a model’s output scales beyond human working memory, the engineering focus must shift entirely from the output to the constraints. We do not read the generated code; we architect the deterministic boundaries that the code must survive. The true discipline becomes defining rigorous type systems, establishing impenetrable testing suites, and configuring automated execution environments. In a mature agentic workflow, an engineer does not debug the syntax of a failing script; they deploy a secondary model instance—perhaps running locally via vLLM for high-throughput inference—to evaluate, critique, and iteratively correct the primary model's output against a strict compiler standard. The system debugs itself.

To insist that the software engineer must remain the ultimate manual debugger demonstrates a dangerously high time preference. It trades the immense leverage of automated, scalable verification for the immediate, tactile illusion of control that comes from reading a pull request. Optimizing for human review bottlenecks the execution speed of the machine to the reading speed of a primate.

Ultimately, the belief that reviewing and debugging are the skills of the future is merely the ego of the traditional programmer refusing to let go of the syntax. The true revelation of models at the scale of Opus 5.5 is that they force a ruthless abstraction layer upon the industry. The human is finally freed from the minutiae of the compiler and the debugger, transitioning permanently from a writer of localized instructions to an architect of autonomous, self-correcting systems.

据《金融时报》，亚马逊正洽谈把约 80 亿美元 Nvidia 芯片放入特殊目的载体，再租回使用。交易尚未完成；真正值得追的是折旧与残值最后由谁承担。

3｜4999 美元的本地 AI，能算过云端吗？
NVIDIA 公布 64GB DGX Spark，10 月 23 日起售，4999 美元起。官方称单机可运行最高千亿参数模型。能跑不等于划算，我更想看每个 Agent 任务的实测成本。

6｜一次验证通过，账号就真的安全吗？
Cloudflare 新调查界面把登录、注册、设备和网络线索按账户串起来，目前只面向 Early Access 客户。对 Web3 平台的启发是：登录之后仍要识别异常，也要给误判留下申诉出口。

我的判断：AI 下一轮竞争，不只看谁的模型更强，也看谁能长期负担成本、分配风险、建立信任。你最想追哪条后续？

千亿收入与百亿亏损的冰火两重天，拆解AI赛道的真实商业密码

最近，路透社独家曝光了Anthropic的IPO招股草案。这份文件堪称全球人工智能赛道最权威的“体检报告”，首次完整呈现了头部大模型公司的真实账本，没有修饰，只有赤裸的数据。

作为由OpenAI核心团队创立的全球第一梯队企业，Anthropic的招股书彻底揭开了AI行业的三大核心矛盾。

第一，需求端彻底爆发，但增长含金量极高。2024年营收仅3.86亿美元，2025年直接飙升至45.9亿美元，暴涨12倍。进入2026年，年化运行收入已突破650亿美元，年底有望冲击千亿规模。需要纠正一个误区：千亿是年化运行率，并非实际到账收入。但更关键的是，其超八成收入来自企业按量调用，而非普通用户订阅。这证明AI已全面进入金融、科研、开发等核心产业场景，产业需求用百亿级付费规模给出了“AI能落地”的最终答案。

第二，亏损结构揭示商业模式的本质改变。AI早已不是轻资产的互联网生意。尽管420亿美元年度净亏损中，有340亿是股权估值变动的纸面会计亏损，但剔除虚账后，真实的经营性亏损仍高达80.6亿美元，较去年翻了近三倍。亏损根源直指行业核心痛点：算力重资产。2025年，算力与基础设施支出高达73.3亿美元，占运营成本的58%。每一次调用都在消耗GPU和电力，这与传统软件“一次开发、终身复用”的模式截然相反。尽管规模效应初现，算力支出与营收比从2024年的6倍降至2025年的1.6倍，但行业无解的现状是：增速再快，也跑不赢算力开支的增速。

第三，刚性负债与弹性收入的致命错配，是最大的系统性风险。招股书显示，公司签下了总价值5180亿美元的算力长期合同，大部分为不可取消的刚性负债，企业必须提前锁定产能，否则未来业务将直接卡死。然而，收入端却极度脆弱：两大客户贡献近25%营收，且绝大多数企业客户没有长期锁价合同，预算随时可能缩减。

至此，AI赛道的核心矛盾彻底曝光：供给端是巨额刚性长期投入，需求端是随时波动的市场化订单。这不仅是Anthropic的挑战，更是所有大模型公司共同的宿命。市场不需要再争论AI的价值，但如何破解这场“卖水人”的困局，目前还没有标准答案。

2025年起，我反复强调的四个原则：

原则1，时代的第一性原理：LLM一定会越来越聪明，benchmark越来越高，context window越来越大，reasoning越来越长，价格越来越便宜，inference速度越来越快，

这是scaling law今天依然持续的具体方向，不用你质疑，这是你唯一的信仰和行业最大共识。

原则2， 管理学设计红利：从我提出“自动编程机”、行业提出vibe coding、SWE-Agent以来，从cursor到manus到metaGPT到claude code，

人们逐渐把LLM Agent抽象成人，把软件管理、工程管理、管理学等等所有方法论直接套在multi agent workflow上面，严格按照人类管理学的方式去拆分、review、执行、反馈、循环，

这一波很快红利也吃完了，因为 a. LLM Agent毕竟不是人，存在着memory有限、执行力有限、function calling工具有限等等局限；b. 人类用于管理学的各种方法，直接套在LLM Agent上有利有弊，红利迅速挖掘完，剩下的弊端大量存在，比如过度交流、七手八脚、随时停工等等。

原则3，LLM Agent的职位和定位：绝大多数人，把claude code当做一个工具，最终的产品是用工具来完成的，最终的代码也是人与SWE Agent一步一步interactively迭代产生、迭代review、迭代部署的，

而我反复告诉过所有人，也是我又一条首次提出的原创观点，multi agent未来越来越会变成本身的一个runtime，这个runtime就运行在production里面，产品和面向的对象消费的，不只是软件或者SaaS本身，而是这个runtime实时产生的内容，

所以claude code/opencode/codex/openclaw这些agent，本身将会越来越多地被嵌入到产品本身，在产品关键逻辑和决策中发挥作用，

而绝对不仅仅停留在开发层面，把产品仅仅局限在SWE Agent单向产出和部署的代码和服务上。

原则4，也是我一直强调的，就是当人们试用了SWE Agent这种强大工具之后，人们还有哪些low hanging fruits可以寻找？SWE Agent目前最适合解决哪类问题？

我反复讲过的一点是，对于一个设计复杂、环境复杂、场景复杂、用户复杂、体量复杂、范式复杂、一切开放、一切无解的超级复杂系统，这并不是SWE Agent最擅长的领域，相反这些场景需要人去和环境、客户、场景、性能一点点迭代才能打磨好的产品，

比如微信的100种功能，Facebook的一大堆功能模块和十几年来迭代出来的极其复杂的infra，支付宝后面成千上万的基金和风控，这些都不是AI Agent能一次性解决的问题，相反这些场景和问题不仅高度开放，更高度依赖人的观察、人的设计、人的反馈、人的定义。

AI Agent最适合的场景，甚至是我原创提出goal driven（https://t.co/mJld9XcBjp）设计的最适合场景，在不考虑token使用量和时长的条件下（参照第一性原理，这些成本必然会越来越低），必然同时具有如下特点：

a. 定义简单、干净、封闭（一道数学系、一个确定性最小系统、一个编译器、一种算法、一个lean证明、一个电路或者信号模拟、蛋白质模拟和预测、CAD设计与仿真、游戏关卡测试、行为经济学仿真，都是well-defined problems，都有非常明确且封闭的边界）

b. 解决问题的搜索空间巨大（可能有100~10万种天马行空的解决方案，并且绝大多数都是错的）

c. 容易验证，容易verify，验证的成本是设计成本的千分之一（比如编译器，设计可能需要几万行甚至几十万行，验证只需要2000个test case全面覆盖，或者一道数学题，解决需要100步，验证答案只需要带入或者lean编译这一步）

当然，写一段简单的代码，定义一个封闭、完整、定义完全的编程问题，符合上面这些定义，

但是设计一套巨大、复杂、开放、与现实世界深度绑定、高度耦合的系统，让这个系统复杂迭代、添加功能、沟通、review、工程管理、产品管理，这些问题都远远超出这个范畴，很明显是不符合这个要求的。

人们未来探索这些multi agent产品和场景的最关键出路，在于继续挖掘这一类问题，而不是盲目把agent比作一个人，乱套各种管理学方法。

$PLTR just partnered with Armada to accelerate sovereign AI infrastructure, and I don’t think many people fully realize what this really means.

Palantir is increasingly covering both ways a customer might want to run sovereign AI:

(1) If you want your compute in an AI data center, Nebius is Palantir’s preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner, bringing its compute and inference endpoints directly inside the Palantir enterprise perimeter.

(2) If you want the compute physically on your own premises, Armada can now effectively bring the data center to you, with Palantir integrating its entire Sovereign AI OS, built on AIP, Ontology, Foundry, and Apollo, onto Armada’s modular Galleon data centers.

So the customer can now own and control the compute, data, model weights and physical infrastructure, without relying on an external cloud. The systems can even operate fully air-gapped where required.

As Karp put it:

“Sovereignty is not something you rent. It is owning the weights, the data, and the hardware those models run on, and knowing where that hardware was built.”

And perhaps the most interesting part is time to local tokens. 

Palantir says this infrastructure can be deployed in months rather than years, bringing new AI capacity to sites where power is already available. 

But this last part matters a lot here. You can bring a modular AI data center to a customer relatively quickly. But you cannot magically create 10 or 20 MW of grid capacity where none exists.

And this is where something like Bloom Energy’s fuel cells could become very interesting. Bloom isn’t currently a Palantir or Armada partner, as far as I can find, but the fit is very natural and easy to see.

If a customer wants its own AI infrastructure but can’t get enough power from the grid quickly enough, onsite generation could remove another major bottleneck. Bloom is already doing exactly that elsewhere in AI infrastructure, including with Nebius. 

So I wouldn’t be surprised to eventually see something like Bloom become another preferred Palantir partner, this time on the power side.

Or maybe Palantir is already thinking one step further. CTO Shyam Sankar personally has a stake in nuclear startup Valar Atomics, which is already working with NVIDIA on pilot projects for nuclear-powered AI infrastructure.

This is somewhat speculative on my part, so take it with a grain of salt, but the takeaway is that this company always seems to be thinking one or two steps ahead.

Now step back for a second and look at the pieces Palantir is putting together in its sovereign AI Lego:

Customers that want AI cloud infrastructure have a path through Nebius, and customers that want to physically own and control their infrastructure on-premises now have a path through Armada.

And Palantir doesn’t need to interact with the physical world directly. It doesn’t need to manufacture GPUs, build data centers, or generate electricity.

Instead, it creates a living model of that physical world through the Ontology and positions itself right at the center of it, essentially becoming the zero coordinate of sovereign AI.

The GPUs can come from NVIDIA. The compute can live in a Nebius data center or an Armada box on the customer’s own premises. The power can come from the grid or, potentially, onsite generation.

This makes Palantir’s Sovereign AI OS essentially the operating system of this new sovereign AI world, where enterprises increasingly want to build, own, and control their own intelligence, distilled from years of hard-earned institutional knowledge, rather than hand it over to someone else.

Or, in Palantir’s own words:

“The Sovereign AI revolution is here, and it runs on the Palantir Sovereign AI OS.”

In ancient times, they used to say all roads lead to Rome. In AI, it increasingly feels like all roads lead to Palantir.

Creating a ChatGPT Plugin might just be the best investment you can make as a business in 2026. 

Here's why: ChatGPT and Codex will now suggest Plugins to you in the middle of a conversation.

The flips the traditional user journey for plugins on its head:
- Before: A user had to already know about your product and go enable it as a plugin.
- Now: Based on the user's intent and the problem they're trying to solve, ChatGPT and Codex suggest which plugins might be useful to them.

In other words, OpenAI is playing aggregator. That makes it a new discovery channel for new products and services.

I can see this going two ways:

(1) It works really well
- I discover new products I didn't know I needed, right when I have the problem.
- I think this will be the case for most consumer apps and services.

(2) It gets in the way
- This might be what happens in B2B settings
- I've already committed to and paid for a set of tools for my business, and I just want to use those plugins without being pitched new ones.

Your AI agent is snitching on me.

In exchange for small conveniences, a transcribed meeting or help planning an evening, you are unilaterally donating your friends' thoughts, ideas and privacy to a company.

Right now, bringing an AI agent into a conversation quietly strips privacy from everyone talking to you. They never opted in and don't know it's happening.

And we're barely in Chapter 1.

Remember the arc of social media? First it just helped connect us with friends. Then showed us increasingly targeted ads. Then nudged us to hate & fear each other.

We don't know the beast these cute creatures will grow into, but the corporate species and it's predatory imperative is  recognizable.

The trust contract at the core of friendships, relationships, and even colleagues talking is at stake.

We need to have the conversation, together, about honoring interpersonal privacy.

A huge part of it will be how to protect the intent conversation partners when we use private messaging.

Right now when you message someone on WhatsApp with disappearing messages, the presumption is that the message will, indeed, disappear. But what happens when this person is using an agent that keeps a copy?

This will be hard. App developers, frontier labs, and OS developers all have powerful incentives to let agents in... 

But there are also promising directions like local inference, and confidential inference (e.g. TEEs) that balance some benefits with the enormous potential for privacy downsides when the data is handed over to a 'trust me' company.
